One might, first of all, object that it is very strange that we generally do not find in the interior of these great circles any serious inequalities of the ground, any mountain resembling those of the outer rampart. One would expect to find regular concentric rings at various distances from the centre, marking the progressive decrease of the eruptive phenomena in the course of geological time. But there is nothing of the kind!

The theory of volcanic origin has been abandoned, for it was found that the craters were too large to have been produced by the action of lava.  Moreover, the craters are not always circular, as would be expected if they had been formed by the eruption of lava.  They are often irregular, and sometimes even elongated.  The theory of meteoric origin is now generally accepted.  It is supposed that the moon was once a planet, but that it was broken up by some violent cause, and that the fragments thus formed were drawn together again by gravitation, and became the moon.  These fragments were probably composed of metallic iron, and when they fell upon the moon's surface, they produced the craters.
